sentences.text: Alvarezsaurus was a small, bipedal theropod dinosaur.
This animal measured between 1 and 1.4 meters in length and weighed about 3 kilograms.
Its foot structure was unique among relatives because metatarsal III was the longest bone, followed by an unusually long metatarsal IV.
The creature possessed a beak and developed feathers covering its body.
The leg structure suggests the animal was capable of running fast.
Despite having a beak, sharp teeth indicated it was a carnivore likely feeding on lizards, insects, and small mammals.
The type specimen was discovered in March 1989 by Jorge Calvo while prospecting along the south coast of the Río Neuquén.
While bone fragments were common finds, the initial discovery involved a 5 cm long white bone fragment found near a light post.
After uncovering part of the fossil, Jorge Calvo confirmed it was the leg of an animal with hollow bones.
Alvarezsaurus was named by José Bonaparte in 1991 in honor of the historian Don Gregorio Alvarez.
In 1991, José Bonaparte published the description of Alvarezsaurus in the Revista del Museo de Ciencias Naturales de Buenos Aires, dedicating the species A. calvoi to Jorge Calvo.
Alvarezsaurus is considered a basal member of the Alvarezsauridae family, preceding better-known relatives like Mononykus and Shuvuuia.
Alvarezsaurus has been classified as either a non-avian theropod or a primitive bird, but the theory linking Alvarezsauridae closely to modern birds remains controversial despite earlier support.
It was once believed that Patagonian Alvarezsaurus taxa were the most basal in their family, but this was refuted by the discovery of the more basal genus Haplocheirus in China.
Alvarezsaurus lived in Argentina approximately 86 to 83 million years ago during the Late Cretaceous.
Alvarezsaurus lived during the Late Cretaceous, between 89 and 85 million years ago in the Coniacian stage, in what is now South America.
The fossil record for Alvarezsaurus dates from 85.7 to 83.6 million years ago during the Santonian age.
